title: Characterisation of a satellite-to-ground channel for continuous variable quantum key distribution protocol
authors: Emma Tien Hwai Medlock, Vinod N. Roa, Timothy Spiller, Rupesh Kumar
abstract: In space based quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols, the quantum channel will be dynamic in nature and the channel loss will change with respect to the zenith angle. In the context of continuous variable (CV)-QKD, this will cause issues with parameter estimation and for a transmitted local oscillator in particular it will also fluctuate the shot noise. Therefore, it is vital to characterise this channel loss and the sources of this loss. In this paper the varying channel loss is characterised under practical assumptions. This is shown for various different scenarios, turbulence strengths, as well as wavelengths. This work shows, for the channel parameters considered, it is possible to generate a positive secret key if restricted Eve security assumptions are made.
summary: This paper characterizes the complex, zenith-angle dependent channel loss for continuous variable QKD links between satellites and ground stations. By modeling atmospheric turbulence effects, the authors demonstrate that despite these significant fluctuations in signal attenuation, secure key generation remains feasible under specific security assumptions.
main_problem: The primary challenge is characterizing the dynamic channel loss experienced by continuous variable (CV)-Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) signals transmitted from a satellite to a ground station.
main_result: Despite the highly dynamic nature of the channel loss due to changing zenith angles, the authors show that it is possible to generate a positive secret key rate under restricted security assumptions.
method: The methodology involves modeling the varying channel loss by integrating atmospheric structure parameters (like weighted C2^N) over the path length determined by the zenith angle. Key rates are then calculated based on these characterized loss parameters.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a space-based CV-QKD link, specifically referencing parameters for the SPOQC mission at 550 km altitude using 1550 nm wavelength light.
key_observables: Channel loss (dynamic), achievable secret key rate, weighted C2^N profiles, and turbulence strengths.
important_parameters: Satellite altitude (550 km), Wavelength (1550 nm), Zenith angle range ($-30^\circ$ to $+30^\circ$), Turbulence regimes (low, medium, high).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on restricted Eve security assumptions and models the channel loss based on practical atmospheric propagation assumptions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the QKD exchange window over zenith angles; Figure 2 shows profiles of C2^N versus altitude and weighted C2^N versus zenith angle, mapping turbulence strength.
paper_structure: The paper first characterizes the varying channel loss under practical assumptions for different turbulence strengths (Section II), followed by an analysis of the resulting achievable key rates for the CV-QKD protocol (Section III).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenges of implementing quantum communication in dynamic, real-world environments like space, which is a major focus area bridging quantum optics and applied physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Satellite pass over the OGS. Here, the CV-QKD exchange occurs between zenith angles −30◦and +30◦. For this scenario, the satellite will have an altitude of 550 km.

Figure 2: C2 N profiles as a function of altitudes (shown on the top) and the weighted C2 N profile for 550 km downlink as a function of zenith angles (shown on the bottom). Here the power law parameter for day time pday = 1.33 was used, random background turbulence parameter M = 1, root-mean-square high altitude wind speed vw = 21 m/s, and with the initial turbulence strengths as seen in the parameter table.
Figure 3: Point ahead angle for a given satellite altitude. The PAA changes with increasing altitudes of the satellite, ranging from 250 km to 2000 km. This is a typical range for LEO satellites.

Figure 4: Total upper bound channel loss with differing receiver aperture sizes. This was done for a strong turbulence regime, with a wavelength of 1550 nm, a transmitter aperture of 8 cm, a pointing error at the satellite of 4 µrad, and with the satellite at an altitude of 550 km.

Figure 5: The losses as a dependency of wavelength at the zenith is plotted. Here the atmospheric absorption lines have not been taken into consideration. The losses are plotted for a receiver aperture of 60 cm with 30% obstruction, a transmitter aperture of 8 cm, a pointing error at the satellite of 4 µrad, and with the satellite at an altitude of 550 km. This is the loss for a Gaussian modulated CV (GMCV) QKD protocol. For DV-QKD, there will be additional losses due to phase error [50–52] that GMCV does not need to consider as the transmitted local oscillator will experience the same phase drift as the quantum signal [53–55].
